stages.title: Welcome to your CSS Trader Passport
body: CSS is governance-first decision support. It studies markets, explains what it sees and, when you want it to, proposes trades as CSS Trade Cards.

points.title: Discover
points.text: CSS surfaces opportunities and analysis. Every decision is yours.

points.title: Confirm
points.text: CSS proposes governed Trade Cards. Nothing happens unless you confirm it.

points.title: Auto (separate approval)
points.text: Governed automated execution, only where it is permitted and separately authorised. This questionnaire never switches it on.

stages.title: A quick knowledge check, not a test
body: A few short questions help CSS decide which explanations to show you.
There is no pass mark. 'I'm not sure yet' is always an option and simply points you to the right lesson.

questions.prompt: What does a limit order do?

options.label: Fills immediately at whatever the market price is
Fills only at your chosen price or better
Closes a trade automatically after a loss

questions.explain: A limit order sets the worst price you accept. It may not fill at all.
questions.purpose: Checks your familiarity with order types, so CSS explains only what is new. It is not graded against you.

questions.prompt: A stop-loss order is mainly used to…

options.label: Limit a loss by exiting once a price is reached
Increase position size when price falls

questions.explain: A stop triggers an exit at a level you set. In fast markets the fill can be worse than the stop price.
questions.purpose: Checks your familiarity with stop orders, so CSS explains only what is new. It is not graded against you.

questions.prompt: With a $10,000 account and a 1% risk rule, the most you plan to lose on one trade is…
questions.explain: 1% of $10,000 is $100. Position size is then set so that hitting your stop loses about that much.
questions.purpose: Checks your familiarity with position sizing, so CSS explains only what is new. It is not graded against you.

questions.prompt: A trade risks $50 to make $150. Its reward-to-risk ratio is…

options.label: It depends on the win rate only

questions.explain: $150 ÷ $50 = 3. A good ratio still needs a sensible win rate to pay off over time.
questions.purpose: Checks your familiarity with risk reward, so CSS explains only what is new. It is not graded against you.

questions.prompt: Higher volatility usually means…

options.label: Larger and faster price swings, up and down

questions.explain: Volatility measures how widely prices move. It widens both gains and losses.
questions.purpose: Checks your familiarity with volatility, so CSS explains only what is new. It is not graded against you.

questions.prompt: An account falls from $12,000 to $9,000 before recovering. The drawdown was…
questions.explain: Drawdown is the fall from a peak: $3,000 ÷ $12,000 = 25%.
questions.purpose: Checks your familiarity with drawdown, so CSS explains only what is new. It is not graded against you.

questions.prompt: Diversification aims to…

options.label: Reduce the impact of any single position going wrong

questions.explain: Spreading exposure lowers the damage one position can do. It cannot remove market-wide risk.
questions.purpose: Checks your familiarity with diversification, so CSS explains only what is new. It is not graded against you.

questions.prompt: You hold three different tech stocks, each 20% of your account. Your exposure to the tech sector is…
questions.explain: Three positions in one sector add up: 3 × 20% = 60% exposure to that sector.
questions.purpose: Checks your familiarity with portfolio exposure, so CSS explains only what is new. It is not graded against you.

stages.title: Two kinds of trades, kept apart

points.title: A CSS idea
points.text: CSS proposes a Trade Card. You choose whether to trade it. If you do, it is recorded as a CSS-attributable trade, linked to that card.

points.title: Your own idea
points.text: You place a trade without a CSS recommendation. It is recorded as your own trade, in your independent results.

body: Your dashboard will show three numbers: profit or loss from CSS-attributable trades, profit or loss from your independent trades, and your combined account result.
stages.callout: A CSS recommendation is not a guaranteed profit, and the decision to trade is always yours.

stages.title: Before your Passport
body: If you change a recommendation in a way that alters its risk or idea, it is labelled as modified. If the origin of a trade can't be proven, it is held for review rather than guessed.
These confirmations are for onboarding only. They do not replace the CSS Terms or the Trading Risk Disclosure, which you accept separately.
